description: MIT math and AI student building the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a browser tool that compares lunar landing sites and dates. It shows the Sun and Earth against real LOLA terrain horizons, counts down to sunset and Earthset, and scores a surface stay for power and direct-to-Earth contact. A working version is already live. Looking for teammates in web design, data visualization, or lunar science to help polish the demo and presentation.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser tool that lets mission planners, teachers and the public compare up to three lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. For each site it shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, counts down to the next sunset and Earthset, and scores a surface stay for power and direct-to-Earth contact. A landing window finder scans 2025 to 2032 for dates that meet the user's limits, and a south pole map shows live terrain shadows. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL's DE440 ephemeris and agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.001°. Horizons are ray-traced over LRO LOLA elevation maps.
details:
The tool answers one question for up to three sites at a time: "If we land here, at this time, will we have power and a line to Earth, and for how long?"

Features:

  • Site comparison: 22 curated sites (7 Artemis candidate region points, 5 south polar mission sites, 10 Apollo, far-side and other landers) plus any custom coordinates.
  • Horizon panorama per site: the 360° terrain silhouette, the Sun's path for the stay and the month, and the Sun and Earth drawn to angular scale, with Earth's phase.
  • Countdowns to the next sunset or sunrise and Earthset or Earthrise.
  • Stay scoring: sunlight (share of the solar disk above terrain), longest darkness, Earth view share and longest comms gap, with GO, MARGINAL and NO-GO pills.
  • Lunar month timeline that doubles as a time scrubber.
  • Landing window finder with daily sunlight and Earth strips for every year from 2025 to 2032.
  • South pole map with live terrain shadows for the selected time. Click to place a site.

Apparent Sun and Earth vectors in the Moon mean-Earth frame are computed from DE440 and the DE440 lunar orientation kernels with Skyfield, every 2 hours for 2025 to 2032. Terrain horizons for curated sites are ray-traced over LOLA elevation grids (80 m and 240 m polar, 1.9 km global) at 720 azimuths out to 250 km, on a spherical Moon, from 2 m above the ground. Ephemeris, horizons and a two-tier terrain grid (480 m and 960 m) are packed into one 3.7 MB web page, and all geometry runs in the browser. Artemis regions have no public coordinates, so five points come from a search for the best-lit spot (2027 to 2028) with slope under 8° near each named feature.

Accuracy checks: Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation at the IM-2 site agree with JPL Horizons within 0.001° (Earth within 0.0001°). In-browser horizons for custom sites average 0.7° RMS error against full-resolution horizons at 11 polar sites.

Why it matters: when a launch slips, planners can test a new date or a site 20 km away in seconds instead of working through several specialist tools. The same views show students why the lunar south pole is so hard: the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees, so one ridge decides whether a lander has power.
dataRefs: JPL DE440 planetary ephemeris (de440s.bsp) from NASA NAIF generic kernels: Sun and Earth positions seen from the Moon
LRO LOLA gridded elevation data LDEM_80S_80M, LDEM_75S_240M, LDEM_16 from the PDS Geosciences Node: terrain horizons, map relief, live shadows
JPL Horizons System API: independent check of computed positions
Artemis III Site Selection Update (George, Rubio, Lawrence and Curell, LPSC 2026), NASA NTRS: candidate region names and the 6-day default stay
projectRefs: Peña-Asensio, Neira-Acosta and Sánchez-Lozano (2024), Evaluating potential landing sites for the Artemis III mission using a multi-criteria decision making approach, arXiv:2406.19863 (source of the Nobile Rim 2 and de Gerlache Rim 2 points)
